{{Short description|none}}
In [[three-dimensional space]], applying the [[Mathematical operation|operation]] of [[stellation]] to a [[polyhedron]] extends its [[Face (geometry)|faces]] (or edges and planes) until they generate new [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]] that bound a newly formed figure. Stellation represents the dual [[Group action|action]] to ''[[faceting]]'' a polyhedron.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1948|pages=95}}

Originating from studies of [[Star polyhedron|star polyhedra]] in 14th century [[Europe]], a proper mathematical account of polyhedral stellations was given by [[Johannes Kepler]] in his 1619 classic work, ''[[Harmonices Mundi]]''.{{sfnp|Kepler|1997|loc=Book I: II. Definitions; p. 17}} Progress later ensued on detailing and enumerating stellations of prominent stars, such as the regular [[Kepler-Poinsot]] polyhedra,{{sfnp|Wenninger|1965|pages=244–248}} with developments on different stellation methods occurring in the 1900s,  principally from {{harvtxt|Coxeter|du Val|Flather|Petrie|1938}} and soon afterward, {{harvtxt|Pawley|1975}}.

A short generalized table of the most notable polyhedral stellations belonging to convex [[Uniform polyhedron|uniform]] polyhedra is provided, with complete sets of stellations for the [[Platonic solid]]s (including the [[The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra|fifty-nine icosahedral stellations]]), as well as for select [[Catalan solid]]s (e.g., the [[rhombic dodecahedron]] and the [[rhombic triacontahedron]]). Stellations of non-convex uniform polyhedra of structure with facial planes passing through their centers (i.e., [[Hemipolyhedron#Duals of hemipolyhedra|hemipolyhedral]]), which render unbounded vertices, are also included; these are  ''stellations to infinity'' — per {{harvtxt|Wenninger|1983}} — conforming to extensions on traditional definitions of polyhedra.

== Background ==
=== Star polytopes ===
{{further|Kepler–Poinsot polyhedron#History}}
[[File:Stellated dodecahedra Harmonices Mundi.jpg|right|250px|thumb|The [[small stellated dodecahedron]] (left), and [[great stellated dodecahedron]] (right), as found in ''[[Harmonices Mundi]]'' by [[Johannes Kepler]].{{sfnp|Kepler|1619|loc=pl. V (pp. 58:59)}}]]

Experimentation with [[star polygon]]s and [[Star polyhedron|star polyhedra]] since the fourteenth century AD led the way to formal theories for stellating polyhedra:
{{Bullet list
|14th c. AD: [[Thomas Bradwardine]] was the first to detail studies of star polygons by extending the sides of polygons.{{sfnp|Coxeter|1969|page=37}} 
|15th – 16th c.: [[Charles de Bovelles]] became the first to study star polyhedra.{{sfnp|Chasles|1875|pages=480,481}}
|1509: [[Luca Pacioli]] publishes ''[[Divina proportione]]'', featuring [[woodcut]] illustrations by [[Leonardo da Vinci]] of various polyhedra, including "elevated" polyhedra that have been [[Johnson solid#Naming and enumeration|augmented]] by attaching [[Pyramid (geometry)|pyramids]] to faces, as showcased with the [[stellated octahedron]].{{sfnp|Pacioli|1509|loc=pls. XIX, XX}}{{efn|1=More specifically, Pacioli's "elevation" of polyhedra involved truncating (or [[Rectification (geometry)|rectifying]]) the [[Platonic solid]]s, after-which pyramids of different bases are systematically attached to faces of the polyhedra{{sfnp|Innocenzi|2018|loc=p. 248}} (akin to [[kleetope]]s, augmenting them into a "star-like" polyhedron). In this same work, da Vinci illustrates a concaved [[triakis icosahedron]], which shares its outer shell with the [[great stellated dodecahedron]].{{sfnp|Pacioli|1509|loc=pls. XXV, XXVI }}}} 
|1568: [[Wenzel Jamnitzer]] publishes ''[[Perspectiva Corporum Regularium]]'', with ink [[engraving]]s on paper of different polyhedra, such as figures closely resembling the [[great stellated dodecahedron]]{{sfnp|Jamnitzer|1568|loc=eng. F.IIII}}{{sfnp|Innocenzi|2018|pages=256, 257}} and the [[great dodecahedron]],{{sfnp|Jamnitzer|1568|loc=eng. C.V}}<ref>{{Cite web|last=Hart |author-link=George W. Hart |title=Wentzel Jamnitzer's Polyhedra |url=https://www.georgehart.com/virtual-polyhedra/jamnitzer.html |year=1996 }}</ref> both stellations of the [[regular dodecahedron]].
}}

It was in 1619 that the first geometric description of a '''[[stellation]]''' was given, by [[Johannes Kepler]] in his landmark book, ''[[Harmonices Mundi]]'': the process of extending the edges (or faces) of a figure until new vertices are generated, which collectively form a new figure.{{sfnp|Kepler|1619|loc=Liber I: II. Definitio (pp. 6, 7)}}{{sfnp|Kepler|1997|loc=Book I: II. Definitions (p. 17)}}{{efn|1={{harvtxt|Kepler|1997|loc=Book I: II. Definitions; p. 17}} defines a [[star polygon]] via [[stellation]] of a convex polygon:<br />"Some of these [figures] are primary and basic, not extending beyond their boundaries, and it is to these that the previous definition properly applies: others are augmented, as if it were extending beyond their sides, and if two non-neighboring sides of one of the basic figures are produced they meet [to form a vertex of the augmented figure]: these are called Stars."}} Using this method, Kepler was able to discover the [[small stellated dodecahedron]] and the [[great stellated dodecahedron]].{{sfnp|Wenninger|1965|pages=244}}{{sfnp|Kepler|1619|loc=Liber II: XXVI Propositio (p. 60)}}{{sfnp|Kepler|1997|loc=Book II: XXVI Proposition (pp. 116, 117)}} In 1809, [[Louis Poinsot]] rediscovered Kepler's star figures and discovered a further two, the [[great icosahedron]] and [[great dodecahedron]];{{sfnp|Wenninger|1965|pages=244, 245}} he achieved this by experimenting assembling regular star polygons and convex regular polygons on vertices of the regular icosahedron and dodecahedron (i.e., [[pentagon]]s, [[pentagram]]s and [[equilateral triangle]]s).{{sfnp|Poinsot|1810|pages=39–42}} Three years later, [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy]] proved, using concepts of [[symmetry]], that these four stellations are the only regular star-polyhedra,{{sfnp|Wenninger|1965|page=245}}{{sfnp|Cauchy|1813|pages=68–75}} eventually termed the [[Kepler&ndash;Poinsot polyhedra]]. As with most non-convex polyhedra including stellations and other star polyhedra, the Kepler-Poinsot polyhedra, with regular self-intersecting faces, are now known to be inequivalent to the [[Sphere#Generalizations|topological sphere]] as a [[Simply connected space|simple connected surface]]{{sfnp|Richeson|2007|page=431}} (this is in contrast with the traditional convex [[Uniform polyhedron|uniform polyhedra]] and their corresponding [[Homotopy#Invariance|homotopy invariance]]).{{efn|1=See also, {{section link|Euler characteristic|Homotopy invariance}}.}}

=== Stellation process ===
{{further|Stellation#Stellating polyhedra}}
{{harvtxt|Coxeter|du Val|Flather|Petrie|1938}} details, for the first time, all stellations of the [[regular icosahedron]] with specific rules proposed by [[J. C. P. Miller]].{{sfnp|Coxeter|du Val|Flather|Petrie|1938|pp=7,8}} Generalizing these ([[Stellation#Miller's rules|Miller's rules]]) for stellating any [[uniform polyhedron]] yields the following:{{sfnp|Webb|2000}}

{{Bullet list
|The faces must lie in face-planes, i.e., the bounding planes of the regular [[Polyhedron|solid]].
|All parts composing the faces must be the same in each plane, although they may be quite disconnected.
|The parts included in any one plane must be symmetric about corresponding [[point group]]s, without or with reflection. This secures polyhedral symmetry for the whole solid.
|All parts included in planes must be "accessible" in the completed solid (i.e. they must be on the "outside"). 
|Cases where the parts can be divided into two sets, each giving a solid with as much symmetry as the whole figure, are excluded from consideration; combination of [[Chirality (mathematics)|enantiomorphous]] pairs having no common part (which actually occurs in just one case) are included.
}}

These rules are ideal for stellating smaller uniform solids, such as the regular polyhedra; however, when assessing stellations of other larger uniform polyhedra, this method can quickly become overwhelming. (For example, there are a total of 358,833,072 stellations to the [[rhombic triacontahedron]] using this set of rules.){{sfnp|Messer|1995|page=26}} To address this, {{harvtxt|Pawley|1973}} proposed a set of rules that restrict the number of stellations to a more manageable set of ''[[Stellation#Stellating polyhedra|fully supported stellations]]'' that are [[Convex set|radially convex]],{{sfnp|Wenninger|1983|pages=36, 153}}{{sfnp|Messer|1995|page=27}} such that an outward [[Half-line (geometry)|ray]] from the center of the original polyhedron (in any direction) crosses the stellation surface only once<ref>{{Cite web |last=Webb |title=Stella Polyhedral Glossary |url=https://www.software3d.com/Glossary.php |year=2001 }}</ref> (that is to say, all visible parts of a face are seen from the same side).{{efn|1={{harvtxt|McKeown|Badler|1980}} presented an early computer algorithm to generate and visualize stellations of convex polyhedra, as for the 227 [[Rhombic triacontahedron#Stellations|stellations of the rhombic triacontahedron]] that {{harvtxt|Pawley|1975}} formally described.{{sfnp|Lansdown|1982|page=55}} }}

In the 1948 first edition of ''[[Regular Polytopes]]'', [[Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter|H. S. M. Coxeter]] describes the stellation process as the reciprocal [[Group action|action]] to ''[[faceting]]'',{{sfnp|Coxeter|1948|pages=95}} identifying the four Kepler-Poinsot polyhedra as stellations and facetings of the regular dodecahedron and icosahedron.{{sfnp|Cundy|1949|page=48}}{{sfnp|Coxeter|1948|pages=96}} He specifies the construction of a [[star polyhedron]] as a stellation of its ''core'' (with [[Congruency (geometry)|congruent]] face-planes), or by faceting its ''case'' — the former requires the addition of solid pieces that generate new vertices, while the latter involves the removal of solid pieces, without forming any new vertices (the core of a star polyhedron or compound is the largest convex solid that can be drawn inside them, while their case is the smallest convex solid that contains them).{{sfnp|Coxeter|1948|pages=98, 99}}

Lists for polyhedral stellations contain [[Convex polyhedron#Convex polyhedra|non-convex polyhedra]]; some of the most notable examples include:

{{Bullet list

}}

Stellations that topologically do not fit into standard definitions of uniform polyhedra are listed further down (i.e. stellations of [[hemipolyhedra]]).{{sfnp|Wenninger|1983|loc=pp. 101–119}}

"'''Stellation core'''" describes a stellated [[regular polyhedron|regular]] (Platonic), [[Semiregular polyhedron|semi-regular]] ([[Archimedean solid|Archimedean]]), or dual to a semi-regular ([[Catalan solid|Catalan]]) figure.<br />"'''[[Stellation diagram|Face diagram]]'''" represents the lines of intersection from extended polyhedral edges that are used in the stellation process.<br />"'''Refs.'''" (references) such as indexes found in {{harvtxt|Coxeter|du Val|Flather|Petrie|1999}} using the Crennells' illustration notation ('''C'''), and {{harvtxt|Wenninger|1989}} ('''W''').

===Enumerations===
The table below is adapted from research by Robert Webb, using his program [[Stella (software)|Stella]].<ref name="Enumer">{{Cite web |author=Webb |title=Enumeration of Stellations (Research) |url=https://www.software3d.com/Enumerate.php |year=2001 }}</ref> It enumerates fully supported stellations and stellations per Miller's process, of the regular Platonic solids as well as the semi-regular Archimedean solids and their Catalan duals. In this list, the [[elongated square gyrobicupola]] and its dual polyhedron are not included (these are sometimes considered a fourteenth Archimedean and Catalan solid, respectively). The base polyhedron stellation core is included as a ''zeroth convex stellation'' following the Crennells' indexing, with stellation totals the sum of ''[[Chirality (mathematics)|chiral]]'' and ''reflexible'' stellations (a "chiral" stellation is [[Chirality (mathematics)|enantiomorphous]], while a "reflexible" stellation maintains the same group symmetry as its stellation core, yet remains achiral – for a count of these separately, visit the parent source).

"'''Cell types'''" are sets of symmetrically equivalent stellation cells, where "'''stellation cells'''" are the minimal 3D spaces enclosed on all sides by the original polyhedron's extended facial planes.<br />"'''?'''" denotes an unknown total number of stellations; however, the number of reflexible stellations are sometimes known for these (where chiral stellations are excluded).

== Stellations of Platonic solids ==
Only three of the five [[Platonic solid]]s produce stellations: the [[regular octahedron]], [[regular dodecahedron]], and [[regular icosahedron]]. The [[regular tetrahedron]] and [[cube]] are unable to generate stellations when extending their [[Face (geometry)|faces]], since extending their vertices only form one possible [[convex hull]].{{sfnp|Coxeter|1973|page=96}}

=== Stellations of the octahedron ===
{{main|Stellated octahedron}}

The ''[[stella octangula]]'' (or stellated octahedron) is the only stellation of the regular [[Regular octahedron|octahedron]].{{sfnp|Coxeter|1973|page=96}} This stellation is made of [[Dual polyhedron|self-dual]] tetrahedra, as the simplest [[Polytope compound#Regular compounds|regular polyhedral compound]]:{{sfnp|Coxeter|1973|pages=48,49}}

=== Stellations of the icosahedron ===
{{main|The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra}}
{{further|List of Wenninger polyhedron models#Stellations: models W19 to W66}}

[[File:Icosahedron stellation diagram center.svg|upright=0.8|right|thumb|This is the [[stellation diagram]] of the [[regular icosahedron]], with face sets labelled, 0-13.]]

{{harvtxt|Coxeter|du Val|Flather|Petrie|1938}} detailed the stellations of the regular icosahedron with rules proposed by J. C. P. Miller. "'''[[The Fifty-Nine Icosahedra#List of the fifty-nine icosahedra|Cell]]s'''" (du Val notation) correspond to the internal congruent spaces formed by extending face-planes of the regular icosahedron.

A subset of these are illustrated in {{harvtxt|Wenninger|1989}}, alongside constructions for physical models (W19–W66).{{sfnp|Wenninger|1989|pages=34-36,41-65}}

== Stellations of Catalan solids ==
=== Stellations of the rhombic dodecahedron ===
{{further|Rhombic dodecahedron#Stellations}}

[[File:HC R1-1stellation.png|right|220px|thumb|'''''Escher's solid''''', or the [[first stellation of the rhombic dodecahedron]], [[Tessellation|tessellates]] three-dimensional space with copies of itself.{{sfnp|Holden|1971|loc=p. 165}}]]

The [[rhombic dodecahedron]] produces three fully supported stellations, described in {{harvtxt|Luke|1957}}:{{sfnp|Cundy|Rollett|1961|pages=149–151}}<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hart |author-link=George W. Hart |title=Stellations |url=https://www.georgehart.com/virtual-polyhedra/stellations-info.html |year=1996 }}</ref>
{| class="wikitable"

An additional fourth stellation is possible under Miller's rules.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |author-link=Eric W. Weisstein |title=Rhombic Dodecahedron Stellations |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/RhombicDodecahedronStellations.html |year=1999 }}</ref> The [[first stellation of the rhombic dodecahedron]] is notable for being able to form a honeycomb in three-dimensional space, using copies of itself.{{sfnp|Holden|1971|loc=p. 165}}

=== Stellations of the rhombic triacontahedron ===

Of these, the [[compound of five cubes]] is notable for being a [[regular compound polyhedron]]. The [[medial rhombic triacontahedron]] and the [[great rhombic triacontahedron]] are also notable for being star (non-convex) [[List of isotoxal polyhedra and tilings#Isotoxal star-polyhedra|isotoxal polyhedra]].

== Hemipolychrons ==
{{further|Hemipolyhedron#Duals of the hemipolyhedra}}

In {{harvtxt|Wenninger|1983}}, a unique family of stellations with [[Hemipolyhedron#Duals of the hemipolyhedra|unbounded vertices]] are identified.{{sfnp|Wenninger|1983|pages=101–139}} These originate from orthogonal [[Edge (geometry)|edges]] of faces that pass through centers of their corresponding dual [[hemipolyhedra]]. | rowspan="3" |[[Rhombic triacontahedron]]{{sfnp|Wenninger|1983|pages=104, 114}}

This family of stellations does not strictly fulfill the definition of a [[polyhedron]] that is bound by vertices, and Wenninger notes that at the limit their facets can be interpreted as forming unbounded elongated [[Pyramid (geometry)|pyramids]], or equivalently, [[Prism (geometry)|prisms]] (indistinguishably).{{sfnp|Wenninger|1983|loc=pp. 101, 103, 104}} As with their dual polyhedra, these hemipolyhedral stellations are [[List of isotoxal polyhedra and tilings#Isotoxal star-polyhedra|isotoxal polyhedra]] (in their case, ''at [[infinity]]''). The final polyhedron on this list, the [[great dirhombicosidodecacron]],{{sfnp|Wenninger|1983|pages=135,139}} is the only stellation whose dual figure — the last-indexed and most complex non-degenerate [[uniform polyhedron]], the [[great dirhombicosidodecahedron]] (U<sub>75</sub>) — is constructed using a spherical quadrilateral [[Wythoff construction]] (rather than with spherical triangles).{{sfnp|Skilling|1975|page=123}}{{efn|1=The dual to the [[great dirhombicosidodecacron]] is furthermore the ''only'' [[Degeneracy (mathematics)|non-degenerate]] uniform polyhedron that is unable to be constructed using a spherical triangular [[Wythoff construction]]; its coincidental figure (the [[great disnub dirhombidodecacron]]), on the other hand, is dual to the [[great disnub dirhombidodecahedron]], which is the ''only'' [[Degeneracy (mathematics)|degenerate]] uniform hemipolyhedron, also constructed with quadrilateral Wythoff spherical domains.{{sfnp|Skilling|1975|pages=119,123}} }}

The [[Tetrahemihexahedron#Tetrahemihexacron|tetrahemihexacron]] is the only hemipolycron to lack a [[Hemipolyhedron#Duals of the hemipolyhedra|coincidental figure]] arising from duals of distinct hemipolyhedra with common [[faceting]]s.
